uncited: This family encompasses methods that adapt the domain traversal and data structures of isosurface extraction to handle sparse, hierarchical, or multi-resolution volumetric data, avoiding the memory and computational costs of dense regular grids.

Unlike standard grid-based methods that iterate over fixed arrays, these techniques traverse octrees, sparse point sets, or adaptive mesh refinement (AMR) boundaries, dynamically gathering scalar values and generating geometry only where necessary [S1].

They are distinguished from their siblings by their specific approach to handling topological discontinuities: [Marching Cubes with Octree](1259-marching-cubes-with-octree.md) relies on uniform node sizing to prevent cracks, [Sparse Marching Cubes](3825-sparse-marching-cubes.md) uses dynamic lookup for scattered points, [Hierarchical Marching Cubes Enumeration](5223-hierarchical-marching-cubes-enumeration.md) explicitly separates traversal logic for faces, edges, and vertices to ensure coherence, and [2D Stitching](10249-2d-stitching.md) generates stitch cells to bridge AMR level gaps without subdividing quadrilaterals.

All methods in this family operate on a discretized domain, typically a regular grid (Cartesian, octree, or tetrahedral) where each cell contains scalar values or occupancy states at its vertices or centers.
**Surface Determination**: A criterion is applied to identify surface locations.
In isosurface methods, this involves comparing scalar values against a threshold (isovalue) to detect sign changes or equality [30-isosurface-extraction.md].
In blocky meshing, this involves checking occupancy states or material IDs to identify exposed boundaries [31-blocky-meshing.md].
**Mesh Coherence**: Adjacent primitives are merged or connected to form a coherent mesh, often requiring vertex merging to avoid duplicates and ensure watertightness [30-isosurface-extraction.md].
The need for adaptive grid traversal arises from the limitations of dense regular grids when handling large-scale, sparse, or multi-resolution data.
Early isosurface extraction methods like Marching Cubes [30-isosurface-extraction.md] assumed a uniform grid, leading to prohibitive memory usage for sparse fields.
The integration of octrees with Marching Cubes [S1] allowed for hierarchical refinement, but required careful handling of level discontinuities to maintain mesh coherence.
Subsequent developments, such as Sparse Marching Cubes [S1, unofficial] and Hierarchical Marching Cubes Enumeration [S1, unofficial], further optimized traversal for non-uniform data distributions.

In the context of Adaptive Mesh Refinement (AMR), methods like 2D Stitching [S1] were developed to bridge resolution gaps without introducing topological artifacts, preserving the integrity of the isosurface across varying grid densities.
